groups.C: Routes tied to where the money came from

routes.name: Bank of China: buy USD with documented income, then one wire to your own US account
routes.fits: Yuan you earned in China from work or services (salary, fees and similar: what the rules call current-account income), for which you hold proof of source and Chinese tax certificates.
routes.limit: No yearly quota is stated for a non-domestic individual; the bank converts the amount your documents support.
routes.cost_basis: Bank of China's published USD selling and buying rates (10 Nov 2026) and its published wire fee.
pros: Lowest published all-in cost for larger amounts: the wire fee is capped at ¥410 per wire whatever the size.
No quota: the ceiling is your paperwork, not USD 50,000.
Leaves a clean bank trail that matches what U.S. reporting needs.
cons: Needs proof of source and tax certificates for the whole amount; the bank can ask for more.
Charges by intermediary and receiving banks are not published and are not in the figures.
The exchange rate changes every day; the figures are a dated snapshot.
steps: Collect proof for the amount you want to convert: employment contract, pay records and the Chinese tax payment record that covers that income.
Contract, payslips or bank salary entries, tax payment record
Go to the bank with the passport the account was opened with. Say that you are a non-domestic individual buying foreign exchange with lawful income earned in China (current-account yuan income).
Ask the bank to sell you USD at its posted selling rate and credit your own USD savings account. Compare the rate with the bank's public board that day.
Purchase slip showing rate and amount

Order one outward USD wire from your USD savings account to your own U.S. account (your name, account number, the U.S. bank's SWIFT code and address). Send one wire rather than several small ones: the fee is capped per wire.
Pay the wire fee: 0.1% of the amount (minimum ¥50, maximum ¥260) plus ¥150 cable fee.

Keep the purchase slip and wire receipt. Note the rate and the USD received: you need them for the U.S. exchange-gain calculation, and the China account stays reportable for each year it was over the U.S. thresholds.
Receipts kept with your tax records
routes.headline: All-in bank cost (fee + exchange-rate margin)

routes.name: HSBC China (Premier or Advance): buy USD, then a telegraphic transfer
routes.fits: Same legal basis as A1, for HSBC China Premier or Advance customers.
routes.limit: No yearly quota stated for a non-domestic individual; documents decide.
routes.cost_basis: HSBC China tariff effective 31 Oct 2026: 0.1% (min ¥100, max ¥500) plus ¥120 cable. HSBC's exchange-rate margin is not published where it could be read.
pros: Published, capped fee: ¥220 to ¥620 per wire.
Optional 'Pay Exact' (¥200) so the full USD amount arrives.
Same documents as any bank route.
cons: HSBC's own exchange rate was not retrievable, so its margin is blank and the total is charges only.
Fee is higher than Bank of China's for the same wire.
Other banks' charges are excluded by the tariff.
steps: Collect proof of source and Chinese tax certificates for the amount (as A1 step 1).
Contract, pay records, tax payment record
At an HSBC China branch, buy USD with the yuan, as a non-domestic individual with lawful income earned in China; USD is credited to your HSBC foreign-currency account.
Order a telegraphic transfer in USD to your own U.S. account. Decide whether to add 'Pay Exact' (¥200) so that overseas bank charges are not taken from the amount.
Pay 0.1% of the amount (minimum ¥100, maximum ¥500) plus ¥120 per cable.
Keep the purchase slip and wire advice for the U.S. exchange-gain calculation and account reporting.
routes.headline: Bank charges only (HSBC margin blank)

routes.name: HSBC China Global Transfer to your own HSBC account abroad
routes.fits: HSBC China customers who also hold an HSBC account in their own name outside mainland China.
routes.limit: Same documents as A1 to buy the USD first. Availability for a U.S. destination must be confirmed with HSBC.
routes.cost_basis: HSBC China tariff item 2.2.6.1: free for Private Banking and Premier; USD 20 per transfer for Advance.
pros: Published transfer charge of zero (Premier, Private Banking) or USD 20 (Advance).
Moves between your own same-name accounts.
cons: You must already hold an HSBC account abroad in the same name.
The USD still has to be bought first under the same rules; HSBC's exchange-rate margin is blank.
Whether the service reaches a U.S. HSBC account was not confirmed.
steps: Open or confirm an HSBC account in your own name outside mainland China and link it in HSBC's Global View.
Overseas HSBC account in the same name
Buy USD at HSBC China with the documents for a non-domestic individual (as A1 steps 1 to 3).
Passport; proof of source; tax certificates
Send the USD by Global Transfer to your own overseas HSBC account. Charge: free (Private Banking, Premier) or USD 20 (Advance).
Keep the records for the U.S. exchange-gain calculation; the overseas HSBC account is itself a foreign account for U.S. reporting if it is outside the U.S.
routes.headline: Transfer charge (HSBC margin blank)

routes.name: HSBC China Private Banking (individual): telegraphic transfer
routes.fits: HSBC China Private Banking individual customers.
routes.limit: Same documents as A1.
routes.cost_basis: HSBC China tariff items 2.2.4.1 and 2.2.4.2: issuance and cable are free for individual Private Banking customers.
pros: Published wire charge of zero.
cons: Only for Private Banking customers.
HSBC's exchange-rate margin is blank; other banks' charges are excluded.
steps: Collect proof of source and Chinese tax certificates (as A1 step 1).
Contract, pay records, tax payment record
Buy USD through your Private Banking relationship as a non-domestic individual with lawful income earned in China.
Order the telegraphic transfer to your own U.S. account; issuance and cable are free for individual Private Banking customers.
Keep the records for the U.S. exchange-gain calculation and account reporting.
routes.headline: Bank charges only (HSBC margin blank)

routes.name: Wise: send from your Chinese bank account to your own account abroad
routes.fits: People who are not mainland Chinese, work or worked in China, and hold a China tax record showing tax paid within the last 3 years.
routes.limit: ¥300,000 per transfer from a bank app (¥50,000 from Alipay); total limit equals the after-tax salary your tax records prove; only to an account you own.
routes.cost_basis: Limits published by Wise. Wise's fee and exchange rate are shown only when a transfer is set up, so they are blank here.
pros: No branch visit: pay in by local yuan transfer from your own Chinese bank app.
Uses tax records you may already have.
Pays out to your own bank account abroad.
cons: Only salary-type income covered by tax records from the last 3 years.
¥300,000 per transfer: about 9 transfers for USD 400,000.
Fee and exchange rate are not published in advance.
steps: Check that you qualify: not a mainland Chinese national; you work or worked in China; you hold a China tax record showing tax paid within the last 3 years.
Open a Wise personal account in your own name and start a transfer from CNY to USD, with your own U.S. bank account as recipient.
Upload the tax record when asked. Wise sets a total sending limit equal to the after-tax salary the records show; verification takes 1 to 2 working days the first time.
Pay Wise by a local yuan bank transfer from a Chinese account in your own name to the account details Wise shows (maximum ¥300,000 per transfer).
Wise converts and pays out; repeat for further transfers until your limit is used. Note the quote (fee and rate) of each transfer.
Keep the receipts for the U.S. exchange-gain calculation and account reporting.
routes.headline: Transfers needed (price blank)

routes.name: Send the yuan itself to your own yuan account outside the mainland and convert there
routes.fits: Non-domestic individuals with lawful yuan income in China whose mainland bank offers personal cross-border yuan remittance.
routes.limit: Not established from an official text this session.
routes.cost_basis: No published price was read.
pros: Would avoid buying foreign currency inside the mainland: the conversion happens at the receiving bank.
cons: Only a government-portal republication of a news report was read; the PBOC notice itself was not.
Needs a yuan account outside the mainland; that account is another foreign account for U.S. reporting.
No price, limit or document list could be confirmed.
steps: Ask your mainland bank whether it handles cross-border yuan remittances for individuals ('other current-account' settlement, PBOC notice Yin Fa [2018] No. 3) and what documents it requires.
Do not proceed until the bank confirms eligibility, documents, limits and price in writing; this route is unverified here.
routes.headline: Blank (unverified)

routes.name: USD 50,000 yearly facility (only if the bank treats you as a domestic individual or you hold a Foreign Permanent Resident ID)
routes.fits: A foreigner who has lived in China continuously for at least one year (a 'domestic individual' under the Regulations) or a holder of a Foreign Permanent Resident ID Card.
routes.limit: USD 50,000 equivalent per person per calendar year with ID only.
routes.cost_basis: Bank of China published rate and wire fee, one wire per year.
pros: ID only inside the yearly total: no source documents needed for that part.
cons: Slow: USD 400,000 takes 8 calendar years.
Whether you qualify is decided by the bank; official texts point in different directions for long-resident foreigners.
Borrowing relatives' or friends' quotas is prohibited splitting.
steps: Ask the bank whether its system classifies you as a domestic individual (continuous residence of one year) or whether you hold a Foreign Permanent Resident ID Card.
Residence permit history or permanent resident ID
Inside the yearly USD 50,000 total, buy USD with your ID.
Wire the USD to your own U.S. account (one wire per year keeps the fee at one capped charge).
Repeat each calendar year. Never use another person's quota: splitting to evade the limit is prohibited.
routes.headline: Calendar years needed; all-in bank cost

routes.name: Withdraw cash at ATMs abroad with a mainland bank card
routes.fits: Small amounts, for holders of a mainland card that works at overseas ATMs.
routes.limit: ¥100,000 equivalent per person per calendar year across all cards; ¥10,000 equivalent per card per day.
routes.cost_basis: Limits from SAFE. Card-scheme rate and ATM/issuer fees were not read, so the price is blank.
pros: No paperwork at the bank counter.
Works from outside China.
cons: Hard yearly cap of ¥100,000: about USD 15,000 a year, 27 years for USD 400,000.
Going over the cap suspends overseas withdrawals for that year and the next.
Rate and fees are not published in the sources read.
steps: Ask the card issuer whether the card allows overseas ATM withdrawals and what it charges.
Withdraw at ATMs abroad: at most ¥10,000 equivalent per card per day.
Stop before ¥100,000 equivalent in a calendar year across all your cards.
Use only your own cards: borrowing or lending cards to get round the limit is prohibited.
routes.headline: Calendar years needed (price blank)

routes.name: Buy USD banknotes at the bank and carry them out
routes.fits: Small amounts for a traveller who can first buy the USD lawfully.
routes.limit: USD 5,000 per trip without a permit; above USD 5,000 up to USD 10,000 with a carrying permit from the bank; above USD 10,000 not allowed in principle. Banknote withdrawal up to USD 10,000 per day at the bank.
routes.cost_basis: Bank of China published cash selling rate. Travel cost is not modelled.
pros: No wire fee.
Useful for a few thousand dollars on a trip you are making anyway.
cons: 80 trips for USD 400,000 without a permit (40 with bank permits).
Theft and loss risk; U.S. customs declaration above USD 10,000 per family or group.
The 2003 cash rule's current validity was not re-confirmed.
steps: Buy USD at the bank under the same rules as A1 (documents) or B1 (yearly facility).
Withdraw USD banknotes: up to USD 10,000 per day directly at the bank. HSBC China asks three working days' notice for USD 5,000 or more.
Carry at most USD 5,000 per trip without a permit. For more than USD 5,000 and up to USD 10,000, ask the bank for a carrying permit before you travel.
Entering the U.S. with more than USD 10,000 in total for your family or group: file FinCEN Form 105 with U.S. Customs.
Deposit in your U.S. account and keep the purchase slip for the exchange-gain calculation.
routes.headline: Trips needed; exchange-rate margin

routes.name: Carry yuan banknotes out and exchange them abroad
routes.fits: Very small amounts.
routes.limit: ¥20,000 per person per trip.
routes.cost_basis: Limit from the PBC's explanation of the adjustment. The price of exchanging yuan notes abroad was not read.
pros: No bank step in China.
cons: ¥20,000 per trip is about USD 3,000: 134 trips for USD 400,000.
Exchange price abroad is unknown and blank.
The limit comes from a 2004 official Q&A, not the announcement text.
steps: Withdraw yuan cash and carry at most ¥20,000 per person per trip.
Exchange at a bank or licensed exchange abroad and keep the receipt showing the rate.
Entering the U.S. with more than USD 10,000 equivalent in total: file FinCEN Form 105.
routes.headline: Trips needed (price blank)

routes.name: Change back unused yuan that you originally exchanged from foreign currency
routes.fits: Yuan that you obtained by exchanging foreign currency and did not spend.
routes.limit: With the original exchange memo: within 24 months of the exchange. With ID only: USD 500 equivalent per day (USD 1,000 airside before departure).
routes.cost_basis: Bank of China published selling rate.
pros: ID only for small daily amounts.
With the original memo the unused amount can be changed back.
cons: Only for yuan that came from foreign currency you exchanged; not for salary or other yuan income.
USD 500 per day is 800 days for USD 400,000.
The memo expires 24 months after the original exchange.
steps: Find the original exchange memos (兑换水单) for the foreign currency you converted into yuan; check they are less than 24 months old.
At the bank, present your passport and the memo and change the unused yuan back into dollars.
Without a memo: at most USD 500 equivalent per day with your passport, or USD 1,000 equivalent airside before departure.
routes.headline: Days needed under the ID-only rule

routes.name: Pay U.S. tuition directly from China (HSBC International Education Payment)
routes.fits: Education payments only, for HSBC China customers.
routes.limit: Limited to genuine education bills; not a general way to move savings.
routes.cost_basis: HSBC China tariff item 2.2.7: free for Private Banking and Premier; USD 7 per payment for Advance.
pros: Lowest published charge for a payment that qualifies.
Pays the school directly.
cons: Only for education-related payments.
Document rules for a non-domestic payer were not confirmed.
HSBC's exchange-rate margin is blank.
steps: Get the school's invoice or fee notice in your or your child's name.
Use HSBC China's International Education Payment platform to pay the school. Charge: free (Private Banking, Premier) or USD 7 (Advance).
Keep the invoice and payment record.
routes.headline: Charge per payment

routes.name: Proceeds of selling your mainland home
routes.fits: A non-domestic individual who sold a home bought in mainland China.
routes.limit: The sale proceeds supported by the contract and the tax-paid certificate.
routes.cost_basis: After approval the bank step costs the same as A1 (Bank of China prices). Chinese tax on the sale is separate (statutory 20% on income from transfer of assets).
pros: A defined route for a large one-off amount.
No original exchange memo needed.
cons: Needs the SAFE office where the property is located to review the documents.
Chinese tax on the sale must be paid and evidenced first.
The source is a 2011 SAFE Q&A; the current handling step was not re-checked.
steps: Complete the sale and pay the Chinese taxes on the transfer; obtain the tax-paid certificate.
Submit to the SAFE branch where the property is located: the foreign-exchange purchase application, the sale contract and the tax-paid certificate for the transfer.
After review, buy USD at the bank with the yuan proceeds and wire it to your own U.S. account (one wire).
Report the sale on your U.S. return; Chinese tax paid on the gain may be creditable.
routes.headline: All-in bank cost after approval

routes.name: Inheritance from a mainland estate (foreign-citizen heir)
routes.fits: A foreign citizen who lawfully inherits assets in mainland China.
routes.limit: The inherited amount approved by SAFE; lump sum allowed.
routes.cost_basis: After approval the bank step costs the same as A1. No government fee is stated in the texts read.
pros: Lump-sum remittance is allowed after approval.
Assets from several decedents can be combined in one application.
cons: SAFE approval at the place of the decedent's registered residence.
Needs inheritance, ownership and tax-payment documents.
Paid only to your own overseas account; no cash.
steps: Obtain the documents proving the inheritance and the decedent's ownership, and the tax-payment certificate from the local tax authority.
Inheritance and ownership documents; tax certificate
Apply to the SAFE branch where the decedent's permanent residence was registered, with a written application, your ID and the documents.
With the approval, the bank sells you the foreign exchange and remits it, in one lump sum or in batches, to your own account abroad. Cash cannot be drawn.
In the U.S.: a bequest of more than USD 100,000 from a foreign estate is reported on Form 3520 for the year received.
routes.headline: All-in bank cost after approval

routes.name: Assets you owned before emigrating (former mainland resident)
routes.fits: A person who emigrated from mainland China and is transferring assets obtained before gaining foreign status.
routes.limit: The amount approved by SAFE; lump sum allowed since 2014.
routes.cost_basis: After approval the bank step costs the same as A1. No government fee is stated in the texts read.
pros: Since 10 Feb 2014 the money can go in one lump sum after approval; the old two-year staging is cancelled.
Notarisation and head-office filing above ¥500,000 are cancelled.
cons: SAFE approval at the place of your original registered residence.
Needs proof that mainland residence was cancelled, ownership documents and tax-payment certificates.
Assets without proof of lawful source are not accepted.
steps: Collect: written application explaining the source of the assets, proof that your mainland permanent residence was cancelled, your foreign residence document, ownership documents and tax-payment certificates.
Application; cancellation proof; ownership and tax documents
Apply to the SAFE branch where your original permanent residence was registered.
With the approval, the bank sells the foreign exchange and remits it in a lump sum or in batches within the approved amount, to your own account abroad.
Keep the approval and wire record for U.S. reporting and the exchange-gain calculation.
routes.headline: All-in bank cost after approval

routes.name: Leave the money in China and spend it there
routes.fits: Anyone who has future yuan costs in China (trips, family support, a property).
routes.limit: None.
routes.cost_basis: No conversion takes place, so there is no conversion cost.
pros: No fee, no exchange-rate margin and no exchange gain is realised.
No documents needed.
cons: The money stays exposed to the yuan exchange rate.
The account stays reportable to the U.S. every year it is over the thresholds.
Does not get you dollars.
steps: Keep the account open and use it for yuan spending in China.
Each year the foreign accounts together exceed USD 10,000 at any time, file the FBAR; file Form 8938 if over its threshold; report the interest on your return.
routes.headline: Conversion cost

routes.name: Wait and convert later
routes.fits: Anyone not in a hurry.
routes.limit: None.
routes.cost_basis: Not a cost that can be computed: future rates are unknown.
pros: May reduce a U.S. exchange gain if the yuan weakens.
Time to assemble documents and fix any U.S. filings first.
cons: The rate can move either way.
Tax records used by some routes age out (Wise needs records from the last 3 years).
Reporting continues while you wait.
steps: Decide a date or rate at which you will convert; meanwhile assemble documents and keep U.S. filings current.
Check the official central parity and the bank board before acting.
routes.headline: Blank (future rates unknown)

routes.name: Splitting the money through relatives' or friends' USD 50,000 quotas
routes.fits: No one.
routes.limit: Prohibited.
routes.cost_basis: Chinese penalty exposure under the Foreign Exchange Regulations.
cons: Evading the limit by splitting is prohibited for banks and individuals.
Fine up to 30% of the amount; 30% up to the full amount in serious cases; criminal liability.
The helpers are exposed too.
steps: Not provided: this route is unlawful.
routes.headline: Chinese fine exposure

routes.name: Underground bank or private swap (pay yuan in China, receive dollars abroad)
routes.fits: No one.
routes.limit: Prohibited.
routes.cost_basis: Chinese penalty exposure under the Foreign Exchange Regulations.
cons: Private or disguised buying and selling of foreign exchange: fine up to 30% of the amount; 30% up to the full amount in serious cases; criminal liability.
No legal recourse if the counterparty keeps the money.
The U.S. receipt has no lawful paper trail.
steps: Not provided: this route is unlawful.
routes.headline: Chinese fine exposure

routes.name: Buying crypto or stablecoins with yuan and selling them for dollars
routes.fits: No one.
routes.limit: Prohibited in mainland China.
routes.cost_basis: The notice sets no fine scale; it refers to other provisions and criminal liability.
cons: Exchange between legal tender and virtual currency is illegal financial activity in mainland China.
Banks and payment institutions may not provide accounts or transfers for it.
Related civil acts can be void and losses are borne by the investor.
steps: Not provided: this route is unlawful.
routes.headline: Chinese fine (blank: no scale in the notice)

routes.name: False contracts, invoices or other untrue documents to buy foreign exchange
routes.fits: No one.
routes.limit: Prohibited.
routes.cost_basis: Chinese penalty exposure under the Foreign Exchange Regulations.
cons: Obtaining foreign exchange with false or invalid documents: fine up to 30% of the amount; 30% up to the full amount in serious cases; criminal liability.
An individual who submits untrue documents can also be fined up to ¥50,000.
steps: Not provided: this route is unlawful.
routes.headline: Chinese fine exposure

routes.name: Carrying cash above the limits without a permit or declaration
routes.fits: No one.
routes.limit: Prohibited.
routes.cost_basis: Chinese penalty exposure under the Foreign Exchange Regulations; U.S. seizure risk.
cons: Carrying foreign exchange across the border against the rules: warning and fine up to 20% of the amount.
Unreported amounts above USD 10,000 entering the U.S. can be seized and forfeited.
steps: Not provided: this route is unlawful.
routes.headline: Chinese fine exposure

routes.name: Using other people's bank cards for ATM withdrawals abroad
routes.fits: No one.
routes.limit: Prohibited.
routes.cost_basis: The circular sets no fine scale; it refers to the Regulations.
cons: Borrowing or lending bank cards to get round the withdrawal limit is prohibited.
Exceeding the yearly limit suspends overseas withdrawals for that year and the next.
steps: Not provided: this route is unlawful.
routes.headline: Chinese fine (blank: no scale in the circular)
